subject: Hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression using INLA?

messages.author: 5124ff9045666052
messages.subject: Hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression using INLA?
parts:
Hello,

I have a 2-level HB logistic regression model (Stan code attached at the bottom). I'm essentially pooling the coefficients of the low-level regression models into Gaussian distributions. The current version has no high-level predictors so it's essentially a random-effects model, but ultimately I would like to replace muBeta with something like Z%*%gamma where Z represents high-level predictors and gamma is the corresponding coefficients. Can you please provide some guidance as to whether the simple, random-effects model or the version with high-level predictors can be implemented in INLA?

Thank you,
Alireza Mahani
------------------------------------

# 2-level random-effect hierarchical bayesian logistic regression model; all low-level coefficients are assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution
# this is similar to the election example from Gelman's textbook (chapter 14), except we have more than just the intercept varying across regression groups
# as a result, the low-level coefficients are represented as a beta matrix (across all groups), or a vector within each group (each row of beta)
data {
  int<lower=0> Ntotal; # total number of observations across all groups
  int<lower=0> K; # number of low-level predictors
  matrix[Ntotal,K] X; # matrix of low-level predictors
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[Ntotal]; # vector of binary response variable across all groups
  int<lower=0> Ngroup; # number of regression groups
  int<lower=0,upper=Ngroup> groupLabel[Ntotal]; # group membership label for each observation
}
parameters {
  matrix[Ngroup,K] beta; # each row is the vector of low-level coefficients for one group
  vector[K] muBeta; # mean of Gaussian prior on beta
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigsqBeta; # variance of Gaussian prior on beta
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[Ntotal] yhat;
  for (i in 1:Ntotal) {
    yhat[i] <- dot_product(X[i],beta[groupLabel[i]]); # following the 'election88' example from Stan repo, we create an auxiliary variable to facilitate expressing conditional of y
  }
}
model {
  for (k in 1:K) {
    for (n in 1:Ngroup) {
      beta[n,k] ~ normal(muBeta[k],sqrt(sigsqBeta[k]));
    }
    muBeta[k] ~ normal(0.0,1000000.0); # non-informative prior on muBeta
    sigsqBeta[k] ~ inv_gamma(0.000001,0.000001); # non-informative prior on sigsqBeta
  }
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(yhat);
}

messages.author: 5124ff9045666052
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression using INLA?
parts:
A more concise, mathematical description of the problem:

A) low-level regression (binary logit): P(y_i=1) = 1/(1+exp(-sum(X[i,k]*beta[G[i],k]))) with i=1,..,N (total number of observations); k=1,..,K (number of predictors); G[] is the group label indicator, i.e. it assigns each observation to one of M groups (used Ngroup in the stan script)
B) high-level regression (linear) / pooling: beta[m,k] ~ N(muBeta[k],sigsqBeta[k]) (we are assuming that each of the K set of M coefficients across all groups have come from a normal distribution with unknown mean and variance)

There are non-informative Gaussian and inverse-Gamma priors on muBeta and sigsqBeta respectively, as seen in the Stan code. This model is an extension of Andrew Gelman's election example in chapter 14 of the multilevel regression book. However, instead of using a few scalar coefficients, only one of which is allowed to vary across groups, here we have a vector of coefficients and allow all of them to vary across groups. The pooling strategy is identical.

I hope this description is more clear.

-Regards

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression using INLA?
parts:
The answer to both of your questions is, as far as I can tell, sort of...

The problem is the number of variance parameters you need. INLA assumes that there aren't too many (say, <10, preferably <5). So versions of this model where all of the sigsqBeta[k] are the same should work. But not when they're different. 

As far as I can see, both high and low level models are possible with this caveat. 

If you want, I can do up an example. (I don't know how important those separate variance terms are to the model)

One small thing: the inverse gamma prior your using (with identical small parameters) is often very informative. It's not a great idea. We recommend an exponential on thr standard deviation, although others recommend using a half Cauchy or a half normal on the sd. 

Hope this helps,

Dan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression using INLA?
parts:
Thank you for your reply, Dan! Regarding the variance of Gaussian prior on beta's, I think in principle they should remain different. This is because these beta's can correspond to predictors of different nature and impact on the response. Certainly scaling of X will make beta's more homogeneous, but not entirely. I would like to take a few days to discuss this with my colleagues and get back to you. Also, if I'm going to trouble you with coding up the INLA version, I might as well ask for the 'full' version where there are high-level predictors (i.e. going beyond a random effects model). So I will probably send you a write-up and Stan code for the full model.

As for your tip about the inverse gamma prior on sigsqBeta, my main motive was to maintain conjugacy. But given that more than 90% of MCMC time here is spent on sampling from beta's, I think breaking conjugacy for sigsqBeta's won't have much of an impact. So I will definitely consider your suggestions. Of course, the simplest non-conjugate prior could simply be a uniform distribution such as [0,1e+6] or something like that, right?

Regards,
Alireza

loghc = "expressiion:

loghc = "expressiion: 
          prec = exp(theta);

    muBeta[k] ~ normal(0.0,1000000.0); # non-informative prior on muBeta
    sigsqBeta[k] ~ inv_gamma(0.000001,0.000001); # non-informative prior on sigsqBeta
  }
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(yhat);
}
